questions.q: Mendel carried out his experiments on:
questions.solution:
The **garden pea** ($\textit{Pisum sativum}$) — well chosen: it has clear contrasting characters, grows quickly, self-pollinates naturally, and can be cross-pollinated by hand.

Careful choice of material is half of a good experiment.

questions.q: In a monohybrid cross between two heterozygous tall plants (Tt), the phenotypic ratio in the F2 generation is:
questions.solution:
$\text{Tt} \times \text{Tt}$ gives TT, Tt, Tt, tt.

Tall : short $= \mathbf{3:1}$ by appearance, while the **genotypic** ratio is $1:2:1$.

The two ratios describe the same four boxes — one counts what you see, the other what is there.

questions.q: The phenotypic ratio in the F2 generation of a dihybrid cross is:
questions.solution:
$\mathbf{9:3:3:1}$.

It is simply $3:1$ happening twice independently, which is exactly what Mendel's **law of independent assortment** says: the two characters are inherited without reference to each other.

questions.q: In humans, the sex of a child is determined by:
questions.solution:
The mother contributes an X chromosome every time. The **father** contributes either X (giving a girl) or Y (giving a boy).

So the sex of the child is decided entirely by which sperm arrives first, and it is a 50:50 chance.

Women have been blamed for the sex of their children throughout history. The biology says otherwise, plainly.

questions.q: A trait that appears in the F1 generation of a cross between two pure-breeding parents is:
questions.solution:
The trait that shows in F1 is **dominant**; the one that disappears is recessive.

The recessive trait has not been lost — it reappears in a quarter of the F2, which is exactly how Mendel deduced that inherited factors come in pairs and stay separate.

questions.q: In a cross $\text{Tt} \times \text{Tt}$, what percentage of the offspring are expected to be short (tt)?
questions.solution:
The four possibilities are TT, Tt, Tt, tt — one in four is tt.

$\mathbf{25}\%$.

questions.q: How many pairs of autosomes are present in a human cell?
questions.solution: $23$ pairs in total, of which one pair is the **sex chromosomes**, leaving $\mathbf{22}$ pairs of autosomes.

questions.q: In a cross $\text{Tt} \times \text{Tt}$, how many of the four offspring in a Punnett square are heterozygous?
questions.solution: TT, **Tt**, **Tt**, tt — $\mathbf{2}$ heterozygotes, which is the '2' in the $1:2:1$ genotypic ratio.

questions.q: In the F2 generation of a dihybrid cross, out of 16 offspring, how many show both dominant traits?
questions.solution: The $9:3:3:1$ ratio puts $\mathbf{9}$ of the 16 in the both-dominant class.

questions.q: What is the probability (as a percentage) that a human child will be male?
questions.solution:
The father's sperm carries X or Y with equal likelihood, so the chance is $\mathbf{50}\%$ for each child.

And it is $50\%$ **every time** — a family with four daughters has exactly the same odds on the fifth child as anyone else. Chance has no memory.

questions.q: State Mendel's three laws of inheritance and explain each briefly.
questions.solution:
**1. Law of Dominance.** When two contrasting factors are present, only one — the **dominant** — shows in the appearance; the other is **recessive** and hidden.

This is why the F1 of a tall $\times$ short cross is entirely tall.

**2. Law of Segregation.** The two factors of a pair **separate** during gamete formation, so each gamete carries only one of them.

This is the most fundamental of the three: it explains why the recessive trait reappears in the F2 after vanishing in the F1. Nothing was blended or lost — the factors were simply travelling together without mixing.

**3. Law of Independent Assortment.** The factors for **different** characters are distributed into gametes independently of one another.

A plant's height tells you nothing about its seed colour — which is why a dihybrid cross gives $9:3:3:1$ rather than $3:1$.

**Why Mendel succeeded** where others had failed: he studied **one character at a time**, used pure-breeding lines, and — crucially — **counted** his offspring in the thousands. He was applying mathematics to biology, which nobody had thought to do.

questions.q: Work out a monohybrid cross between a pure tall pea plant (TT) and a pure short one (tt) up to the F2 generation, showing both ratios.
questions.solution:
**Parents:** TT (tall) $\times$ tt (short).

**Gametes:** all T from one parent, all t from the other.

**F1 generation:** every plant is **Tt** — all **tall**, since T is dominant.

The short character has not disappeared; it is carried, unseen.

**F1 self-pollinated:** $\text{Tt} \times \text{Tt}$.

**Punnett square:**

• T $\times$ T $\to$ **TT** (tall)

• T $\times$ t $\to$ **Tt** (tall)

• t $\times$ T $\to$ **Tt** (tall)

• t $\times$ t $\to$ **tt** (short)

**F2 phenotypic ratio:** 3 tall : 1 short.

**F2 genotypic ratio:** 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt.

**The conclusion that matters:** the short trait reappeared in the F2 after being invisible in the F1. Inherited factors therefore stay **separate and intact** — they do not blend, which was the prevailing belief before Mendel.

questions.q: Explain sex determination in humans with a diagram in words, and discuss why the belief that a woman determines a child's sex is scientifically wrong.
questions.solution:
**The chromosomes.** Humans have 23 pairs: 22 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes.

• **Female:** XX

• **Male:** XY

**Gametes.**

• The mother is XX, so **every egg carries an X**. She has no other option to give.

• The father is XY, so **half his sperm carry X and half carry Y**.

**Fertilisation.**

• X (egg) + X (sperm) $\to$ **XX**, a girl

• X (egg) + Y (sperm) $\to$ **XY**, a boy

**The conclusion.** The mother's contribution is the same whatever the outcome. The sex of the child depends entirely on which of the father's two kinds of sperm reaches the egg first — a 50:50 chance he does not control either.

**Why this matters.** In many societies women have been blamed, abandoned or worse for bearing daughters. The biology is unambiguous: the mother's chromosomes cannot determine sex, because she has only X to give.

India's declining child sex ratio is a consequence of acting on that false belief, and it is why prenatal sex determination is a criminal offence here.

questions.q: Distinguish between acquired and inherited traits, and explain why acquired traits are not inherited.
questions.solution:
**Inherited traits** — present in the genes and passed to the offspring. Eye colour, blood group, the shape of the nose, free or attached earlobes.

**Acquired traits** — developed during an individual's lifetime, in response to use, injury or environment. Muscles built by exercise, a scar, a language learned, the weight gained or lost.

**Why acquired traits are not inherited.** Only changes in the **germ cells** — eggs and sperm — are passed on. Changes in **somatic** (body) cells are not.

Exercising a muscle changes the muscle cells; it does nothing to the DNA in the reproductive cells, and so there is no mechanism by which it could reach the next generation.

**The classic experiment.** August Weismann cut the tails off mice for more than twenty generations. Every generation was born with a full tail. The characteristic was acquired, and it was never inherited, however often it was imposed.

**Why this matters for evolution.** It rules out Lamarck's idea that a giraffe's stretching lengthens its offspring's neck. Evolution works the other way round: variation appears **first**, by chance, in the germ cells — and the environment then selects among what is already there.

questions.q: What is variation? Distinguish somatic from germinal variation and explain the importance of variation for a species.
questions.solution:
**Variation** — the differences between individuals of the same species, in appearance, physiology or behaviour.

**Somatic variation** — arises in the body cells during an individual's life. It affects only that individual and is **not inherited**. A scar, a suntan, a muscle built by training.

**Germinal variation** — arises in the reproductive cells, by mutation or by the reshuffling of genes at meiosis and fertilisation. It **is inherited**, and it is the only kind that matters for evolution.

**Where germinal variation comes from:**

1. **Crossing over** during meiosis, which swaps stretches between chromosomes.

2. **Independent assortment** of the chromosomes into gametes.

3. **Random fertilisation** — any sperm may meet any egg.

4. **Mutation** — a change in the DNA itself.

**Why variation matters.** A species faces a changing world: new diseases, new predators, a shifting climate.

If every individual is identical, a single threat that defeats one defeats all of them. If the population varies, some individuals are likely to survive by chance, and they pass on whatever let them do it.

Variation is a species' insurance policy against a future nobody can predict.
